text: You ran your implementation, and your numbers don't match the paper's. This is the single most common outcome of a real reproduction attempt — and how you respond to it is a bigger test of your research judgment than getting a clean match would have been.

This lesson covers why a mismatch is the expected, not exceptional, outcome of a reproduction attempt, a systematic checklist for diagnosing where a discrepancy came from, the difference between 'my implementation has a bug' and 'the paper's claim doesn't hold,' and how to write up a discrepancy honestly whatever its source turns out to be.

Work through a diagnostic checklist roughly in order of likelihood, cheapest to check first. First, implementation bugs — walk your circuit and code against your methodology document line by line. Second, parameter mismatches — re-check shot count, optimizer settings, and scaling factors. Third, specification gaps you filled in yourself — did a guessed detail matter more than expected? Fourth, hardware or environment differences. Only after ruling out all of these should you consider statistical noise, and only after that, a genuine disagreement with the paper's claim.

It's tempting, especially under time pressure, to interpret a mismatch as an exciting finding — 'I found a flaw in a published paper.' The far more common reality is a bug or parameter mismatch in your own implementation. Treating your own code as the most likely source of error, and only escalating your claim after genuinely ruling it out, is a matter of basic research integrity, not a minor stylistic choice.

In a worked example, you reproduce the GHZ zero-noise-extrapolation case from last lesson and measure a smaller error reduction than reported. Your circuit matches your methodology document, and your shot count and scaling factors match. Then you realize you used linear extrapolation instead of the paper's specified Richardson extrapolation — a gap you missed in the appendix on first read. Re-running with Richardson extrapolation closes most of the gap. The conclusion: an extraction error on your part, not a flaw in the paper's claim — a completely normal, useful outcome to report honestly.

Next lesson's lab walks through a full, realistic reproduction attempt end to end — screening, extraction, running, and diagnosing a discrepancy — using this chapter's full toolkit on one worked scenario.
